title: Relative clauses of characteristic and subordinate clause relationships

objectives.can: Read a relative clause with the subjunctive as describing a kind of person or thing, a purpose or a cause; and say how each clause of a sentence hangs on another.

explanation.summary: A Latin relative clause normally has its verb in the indicative and states a fact. When the verb is in the subjunctive, the clause usually says what kind of person or thing is meant, what someone is for, or why. This lesson names those uses and gives a short method for finding how each clause of a long sentence hangs on another.

sections.heading: Indicative or subjunctive after qui?
body: A relative clause adds a fact about a person or thing already named: *beata uita, quam omnes uolunt*, 'the blessed life, which all people want'. The verb *uolunt* is indicative because the clause simply states what is the case. This is the ordinary relative clause, and it is by far the commonest.

In *omnino qui nolit nemo est*, from the same passage of Augustine, the relative clause has a subjunctive, *nolit*. The clause does not point to some person who does not want the blessed life; it says of what kind nobody is: there is nobody of the sort to refuse it. Writers choose the subjunctive when the clause describes a sort, a purpose or a reason, not a fact about a known individual.

sections.heading: Characteristic: sunt qui, nemo est qui, dignus qui
body: The commonest use is the relative clause of characteristic (grammarians also say 'generic'). It follows an antecedent that is indefinite, general or negative, and above all the phrases *sunt qui*, 'there are people who', *est qui*, *nemo est qui*, *quis est qui*, *non est qui*, *est quicquam quod*. It also follows adjectives like *dignus*, *idoneus*, *aptus*: *dignus qui*, 'worthy to', 'the right sort to'.

Usually the best English is 'there is nobody who would …', 'who is there who would …?', 'such as to …'. The subjunctive does not mean the thing is unreal or uncertain. It marks the clause as a description of the type.

The tense follows the sequence of tenses (see the earlier lesson). After a present main verb the clause usually has a present or perfect subjunctive: *nemo est, qui dormire semper uelit*. After a past main verb it has an imperfect or pluperfect.

sections.heading: Purpose and cause
body: A relative clause with the subjunctive can say what a person is sent, looked for or chosen to do: *miserunt qui adprehenderent*, 'they sent men to seize'. It stands where a purpose clause with *ut* could stand, and the verbs that usually go before it are verbs of sending, finding, seeking and providing. The antecedent may be left out.

A relative clause can also give a reason, or admit a fact in spite of which something is true. Words like *utpote qui* and *quippe qui*, 'seeing that he', 'inasmuch as he', usually mark a reason. Without such a word, you must decide from the sense, and sometimes the clause is both a description and a reason. Do not force a choice where the Latin does not make one.

sections.heading: Subjunctive by attraction and in reported speech
body: Some subjunctives in relative and *quod* clauses are there for a quite different reason. A clause that hangs on a subjunctive or an infinitive, and is closely part of the same thought, may take the subjunctive too. Grammarians call it attraction or 'subordinate clause in indirect speech'. In *ut aperirem codicem et legerem quod primum caput inuenissem*, the purpose clause has *aperirem* and *legerem*, and the relative clause inside it has *inuenissem*: it is a part of what Augustine meant to do, so it follows the mood of the clause it belongs to.

Reasons and reports behave in the same way. *admonuerunt ut redirent, quod iam declinasset dies* gives a reason that is reported (the speakers' reason for urging return), with a pluperfect subjunctive. In later Latin, *quod* followed by the subjunctive also replaces the accusative and infinitive after verbs of hearing and saying: *audieram … quod … admonitus fuerit*.
So a subjunctive in a relative clause is not always characteristic, purpose or cause. Ask first what the clause hangs on.

sections.heading: A method for a long sentence
body: 1. Find the end of the sentence. 2. Mark every finite verb (a verb with a person and a number). 3. Mark the connectives that open a clause: *ut*, *ne*, *quod*, *quia*, *cum*, *si*, *dum*, *quamuis*, *qui*, *quis*, *quo*. 4. Put each clause in brackets and say what it hangs on: the main verb, a noun, or another clause. 5. For each relative, ask whether the verb is indicative (a fact) or subjunctive (a kind, a purpose, a reason, or attraction). 6. Only then translate.

A short example is *nemo est enim qui non habeat quod dimittat*. The main verb is *est*; *enim* tells you the sentence gives a reason for what went before. *qui non habeat* is a relative clause of characteristic on *nemo*, and *quod dimittat* hangs on *habeat*, with the subjunctive of purpose or description: 'nobody lacks something to give up'.

misunderstandings: 'Relative plus subjunctive' does not mean one thing. It may describe a type, give a purpose, give a reason, or merely follow a subjunctive nearby. The antecedent and the main verb tell you which.
The subjunctive in *nemo est qui uelit* is not a wish. The ordinary subjunctive of wish is in a main clause; here the subjunctive marks a description.

Late authors do not always follow the classical pattern. Even where a relative clause names a class of people, Augustine often keeps the indicative, as in *ab eis, qui accessuri sunt ad gratiam tuam*, 'by those who are about to come to grace'. Treat the mood as a guide to the construction, not as a law.
A subjunctive after *quod* is not always a cause. After a verb of hearing or saying it may report what was heard.

deeper.heading: Where grammarians draw the lines
body: Allen and Greenough, Bennett and Gildersleeve all separate the relative clause of characteristic, of purpose and of cause, and they add the clause of result and the concessive relative clause. The lines are not sharp. A clause such as *quatenus qui in sanguinem eius crederent* describes a kind of person and is also part of a clause of purpose. The classification serves reading; it does not divide the Latin as a sharp knife.

examples.analysis: *nemo est* is a main clause, 'there is nobody'. *qui dormire semper uelit* is a relative clause on *nemo*, with the present subjunctive *uelit*. It says what sort of person does not exist: nobody is of the kind to wish to sleep for ever. The antecedent is negative and indefinite, which is where the characteristic subjunctive is at home.

examples.analysis: *condignus … non poterit* says that a man will not be able to be 'worthy'. The relative clause *qui haec … obtineat*, with the present subjunctive *obtineat*, says what he is worthy of: it is the *dignus qui* construction, 'worthy to obtain', 'the right sort of man to obtain'. The subjunctive names the quality, not a fact.

examples.analysis: *utpote* before *qui* marks the relative clause as a reason: the monk was free from all worry 'seeing that' he had been cut off from his father's property. Both the verb of the clause, *esset*, and the adjective *extorris* belong to the reason. The word *utpote* is the signal; without it the same clause could be read as a plain description.

options: It is an indirect question depending on *est*.
The relative clause describes the sort of person after *nemo est*, a negative, indefinite antecedent.
It expresses a wish that nobody may want to sleep for ever.
It is a purpose clause: nobody exists so that he may wish to sleep.
practice.explain: After *nemo est* (and *sunt qui*, *quis est qui*) a relative clause with the subjunctive says what kind of person there is or is not: nobody is of the sort to want to sleep for ever. It is not a wish (that would be a main clause) and not a purpose clause (nothing is being aimed at). There is no interrogative word, so it is not an indirect question.

options: Both subjunctives are wishes, because the sentence urges the reader to give up his property.
*quod dimittat* is the main clause, and *nemo est* is a purpose clause on it.
*qui non habeat* describes *nemo*, and *quod dimittat* hangs on *habeat*: nobody lacks something to give up.
practice.explain: The main verb is *est*. *qui non habeat* is a relative clause of characteristic on *nemo*, and *quod dimittat* is a relative clause hanging on *habeat*. *enim* is a connective that gives the reason for the preceding exhortation. The subjunctives are not wishes.

options: It is part of the purpose thought: the relative clause hangs on *legerem* and takes its mood from it.
It states a fact about a chapter that Augustine had already found.
It describes the sort of chapter the book contained.
It is a cum clause with the relative as its subject.
practice.explain: *inuenissem* belongs to the thing Augustine planned: to read whichever chapter he would find first. The relative clause is subordinate to a subjunctive, so it takes the subjunctive by attraction. It is not a fact about a chapter already found, and no *cum* is present.

options: *uolunt* is in the indicative because it is a present tense and *nolit* in the subjunctive because it is a negative verb.
*qui nolit* is a purpose clause, and *quam omnes uolunt* is a cause.
Both clauses are characteristic, and the mood changes only for variety.
*quam omnes uolunt* states a fact about the blessed life; *qui nolit* describes the kind of person there is not.
practice.explain: The first relative clause says what everyone actually wants: a plain fact, so the indicative. The second, after *nemo est*, gives the sort of person who is not found: a characteristic clause, so the subjunctive. The mood does not depend on tense or on negation.

options: A plain statement about a known speaker.
A relative clause of characteristic: who is there of the sort to tell me?
A purpose clause: who is there in order to tell me?
check.explain: *quis est qui* with a subjunctive is the classical pattern for a clause of characteristic: 'who is there who would say?' The clause is a relative one on the unnamed *quis*, not a purpose clause and not an indirect question: *qui* is a relative, and *quis* is the interrogative of the main clause. The speaker has no particular person in mind.

options: It is a command addressed to the man who obtains them.
It names the cause: he cannot be worthy because he obtains these things.
It says for what the man is worthy: the right sort of man to obtain them.
It states that somebody has in fact obtained these things.
check.explain: This is the *dignus qui* construction, a relative clause of characteristic that names what a person is fit or worthy to do: here, to obtain these rewards by his own merit. The subjunctive gives the quality; it does not report that anyone has obtained them. The clause is not a cause and is not a command.

options: A purpose: he stayed away so as to be cut off from his father's property.
A description of the kind of man who owned his father's property.
A reason: he was free from worry seeing that he had been cut off from his father's property.
A condition: if he were cut off from his father's property.
check.explain: *utpote qui* with the subjunctive introduces a reason for what the main clause says: he had no anxiety, seeing that he had no share in his father's property. There is no *si*, so it is not a condition, and nothing in the sentence is aimed at: the monk was already free from worry.

options: A cause: is there anything in me, since it contains you?
An indirect question: is there anything in me, and what contains you?
A relative clause of characteristic on *quicquam*: is there anything in me of the sort to contain you?
A relative clause of purpose: is there anything in me given so that it may contain you?
check.explain: *est quicquam … quod* belongs with *sunt qui* and *nemo est qui*: the antecedent is an indefinite pronoun in a question, and the clause with *capiat* says what kind of thing is meant. Augustine is asking whether there is anything fit to hold God. The other readings have no support from the words.

options: *ut redirent* is a result clause, and *quod …* is an indirect statement.
Both clauses are characteristic, depending on *admonuerunt*.
*ut redirent* is a request and *quod iam declinasset dies* is a reported reason for it.
*quod iam declinasset dies* is a result clause on *redirent*.
check.explain: *admonuerunt ut redirent* is an indirect command: they urged that they return. The *quod* clause with the pluperfect subjunctive *declinasset* gives their reason, as reported speech: because the day had already turned. Neither clause has an antecedent, so neither is a clause of characteristic.

options: *quam omnes uolunt* states a fact about a known thing; *qui nolit nemo est* describes a type that does not exist.
The difference is only one of word order.
*nolit* is a purpose clause, because nobody wants not to want.
check.explain: A plain relative clause on a definite antecedent (*beata uita*) has the indicative. A clause that follows *nemo est* and describes the kind of person has the subjunctive. The tenses of the two verbs are both present, and word order does not decide the mood.

There is nobody of the sort to hide from your heat.

check.explain: *non est qui* with a subjunctive is another way of saying *nemo est qui*: no one is of the kind who could hide. The clause describes the type, so it is not a purpose clause, and *abscondat* is not a command.

options: A relative clause of characteristic, like *audeat*.
The verb of an indirect question opened by *quare*, dependent on *dicere*.
check.explain: *audeat* is the subjunctive of the clause of characteristic after *quis est qui*. *quare* is an interrogative word and opens an indirect question depending on *dicere*, so *fecerit* is a perfect subjunctive in an indirect question. The sentence thus has two kinds of subjunctive in one line.

options: A wish that someone might copy it for me.
Someone to copy out the Latin apostle for me: a relative clause of purpose.
Someone who was copying the apostle for me already.
The person who copied it, as a known fact.
check.explain: After a verb of looking for (*quaerebam*), a relative clause with the subjunctive says what the person is wanted for: 'someone to copy out'. The antecedent is not yet found, so it cannot be a known fact.

reading.reference: Augustine of Hippo, Confessions 8.12 – Augustine of Hippo, Confessions 8.14
reading.why: Three sections of Augustine's account of the days before the garden. They hold a characteristic clause (*nemo est qui*), relative and *quod* clauses with the subjunctive, and a long sentence that can be bracketed with the method.
